Manganese Road

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Manganese mining - huge profits, but at what cost to our health, environment and infrastructure

Unique Selling Point:
Dirk Jooste is an auto-electrician who was medically boarded at the age of 52. He developed Parkinsonian symptoms or manganism after spending 2 years cleaning air conditioner filters on trucks on Mamatwan mine in Hotazel. Both he and his Occupational Practitioner, Dr Tidu van der Merwe will be interviewed. Manganese is a neurotoxin which is known to cause Parkinsonian symptoms in mine workers with prolonged exposure. Washington University and Wits School pf Public Health published a recent study which found that these symptoms were common in the cohort of 178 miners in Hotazel. Professor Gill Nelson of Wits School of Public Health will discus the study.


Summary:
South Africa produces 80% of the world's manganese, with most of it being exported to China. Millions of tonnes of manganese are transported by road from Hotazel to Nelson Mandela Bay where they are stored in the light industrial area of Markman, before being transferred to Port Elizabeth Harbour by truck in open skips. The dust levels in Markman are already 5 times over the "Take drastic action now" levels. Tests for fugitive dust levels at the entrance to the Port Elizabeth harbour are currently underway. Ronelle Friend from EnviroQuest will discuss the findings. Are locals who live and work in NMB exposed to unacceptable health risks and what are the authorities doing about it? Markman is also home to the Fresh Produce Market as well as the city's abattoir. Other businesses in the area have suffered financial losses because of the dust fallout.
Apart from the health risks there are other environmental considerations: the heavy metals found flowing into the Swartkops Estuary is 6000 times higher than the legal limit. Residents complain about manganese dust in their Jojo tanks which has washed off their roofs and gutters. The find, powder-like dust clogs their swimming pool filters and air conditioners. Tourism is also affected. The Port Elizabeth small boat harbour berths several fishing boats which moor under a cloud of manganese dust. The tourist boats as well as every other sailing yacht in the harbour are discoloured by the black dust. The MSC cruise ships also dock in the harbour and passengers are forced to walk through and breathe in the manganese dust which is all pervasive.
Ironically the MMC for Tourism and Economic Development, Khusta Jack, has admitted that he has a trucking company which is also transporting manganese.

Further information:
Enormous political and financial interests are at stake. United Manganese of Kalahari is one of the biggest mines in Hotazel, and is owned by a joint venture which includes Chancellor House - an investment company which funds the ANC - as well as sanctioned Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg, through his company Renova. One of the richest men in the world, Vekselberg's plane and super yacht were recently seized by European authorities. In 2020 Chancellor House's 22% dividend would have paid out R528 million. This could explain why there is political influence brought to bear on the traffic and law enforcement authorities to give the manganese transporters and manganese handlers a free pass. Hundreds of trucks travel to PE harbour and back every day, 24 hours a day to satisfy the demand for manganese. The national, regional and urban road network is being destroyed by these heavy loads which average over 50 tonnes per truck.
Truck drivers are paid per load and are therefore compelled to work long hours with very little sleep. They live in their trucks, only going home every 3 weeks. They are tired, stressed and in many cases suffering from occupational diseases like high blood pressure and diabetes.

Script:


MANGANESE ROAD SCRIPT

PART 1


V/O: It started by chance – on a potholed road near Hanover in the Karoo. When the 4th manganese truck in as many minutes thundered past us, we grasped the true extent of our viewer’s complaints.

And so began a 2-month long investigation into this mysterious industry.A journey that’s taken us from a baking corner of the Kalahari down the Manganese Road to the dust covered city of Gqeberha.

We visited towns along the way, punch-drunk from the constant battering of 38 tonne trucks. People sent pictures of dust clogging their pools, corroding their homes, discolouring their roofs.

Aubrey: This is a tile that I had spare, dating back 41 years ago, and that’s where we’ve got to today.

V/O; We spoke to scientists and doctors who confirmed the toxic effects of manganese dust.

Prof: Manganese exposure is associated with parkinsonism.

Tidu: You could have two persons with the exact same exposure. Nothing will happen to the one and the other one will die.

V/O: We saw the queue of trucks waiting to offload at Port Elizabeth harbour. But nothing could prepare us for the hellhole that is Markman, the industrial area where manganese is bulk stored.

Chris: What am I going to do? We pay our rates. The roads weren’t like this when we got here.

V/O: And we delved into the ownership of the lucrative mines - and discovered a network of Chinese, Australian, and Russian companies with politically influential local partners.

V/O: This is the Kalahari Basin – home to 80% of the world’s manganese – a key component of steel and lithium batteries. Mines dotted around Hotazel export millions of tonnes to China every year, earning billions of dollars in export revenue.

Link: This is Hotazel, not quite living up to its reputation today, but it is the tail-end of winter. Now, forget the posh office blocks in Sandton, it’s in this far-flung corner of the Kalahari that manganese is creating jobs for thousands and making the mining companies fabulously wealthy. But at what cost?

V/O: Manganese is a neurotoxin and excessive exposure to manganese dust or fumes can cause permanent brain damage. Extreme manganese toxicity results in a condition called manganism.

Dirk: The tremor started first, but slightly. Like for instance I tried to test on a fuse box, I couldn’t do it anymore because I couldn’t pinpoint on the fuse with the tester.

V/O: Dirk Jooste was an auto-electrician, working for a sub-contractor on a mine called Mamatwan. His job was repairing air-conditioners on the big, yellow dump trucks.

Dirk: It’s the old triple 7D CAT machines and it’s a very confined space.
So I had to clean out those evaporators inside, and the only way to do it was by pressurised air. Because it wasn’t a dust as such, it’s like a powder, and the whole cab was full of that dust so, when I was finished at night my teeth, my tongue, everything was pitch, pitch black inside.

Derek: How old were you when the symptoms first started?

Dirk: Derek you must excuse me but my memory is a bit…I can remember my childhood and everything, but my short-term memory about everything is not that good.

V/O: Extreme manganese toxicity results in a condition called manganism.

Dirk: I get angry very quickly, and I wasn’t like that before, never before.

V/O: In 2011, at the age of 54, Dirk was diagnosed with Parkinson’s Disease, but the prescribed medication had no effect at all. He also developed blisters on his hands when in contact with manganese. A dermatologist diagnosed severe allergic dermatitis.

Dirk: His recommendation was to take me off the mine completely, and also out of our office area, because it also happens there, because there’s also a lot of manganese dust.

Derek: How did you feel about leaving the mine area?

Dirk: That was my life. My work was my life. It’s taken away. It’s just taken away.

V/O: In 2013 he consulted Occupational Practitioner Dr Tidu van der Merwe in Kathu.

Tidu: I realised that since he was working in a mining environment that this might not be Parkinson’s but manganism. Manganism, like Parkinson’s, will affect your fine motor skills. So that goes through to balance and activities of everyday life.
But getting to the final and conclusive diagnosis that rests with the neurologists.

V/O: So, Dr van der Merwe sent Dirk to a neurologist but his findings were inconclusive.

Tidu: I’m unsure of the final diagnosis – I’m translating here –it is not suggestive of Parkinson’s Disease.

Derek: In 2013 you were convinced Dirk was suffering from severe manganism. Do you stand by that?

Tidu: I still stand by that.

V/O: But what about the other mineworkers? In 2020 the American Journal of Industrial Medicine published an article on manganese exposure and parkinsonian signs in South African mine workers. The study was a collaboration between Washington University and Wits University.

Prof: We went to Hotazel, to the mines. The Union certainly helped us by putting the word out there that we were doing the research.

V/O: Associate Professor Gill Nelson is an epidemiologist at the Wits School of Public Health.

Prof: We ended up with 187 people eventually, 187 mine workers. So we had people who worked there for a year and then we also had people who’d worked there for, say some close to 40 years.

Derek: So what signs did you look for?

Gill: So we look for Parkinsonian signs which is tremor at rest, balance and stiffness in joints – the conventional Parkinsonian signs.

Derek: What were your findings?

Gill: So about 26% of the participants had Parkinsonian signs which is…

Derek: It’s high?

Gill: It’s very high, we wouldn’t expect that.

V/O: The average age of the miners was 42.

Derek: How concerning are these results in reality?

Prof: So they definitely are concerning, because you shouldn’t have such a high prevalence of parkinsonism in a normal population, so there’s something going on.

Link: South32 is an Australian company with a head Office in Sandton. We wanted to talk to them about the health risks of manganese dust exposure, but they said there was nobody in South Africa to interview. So we offered them a Zoom interview from Australia, but all they did was reply in writing.

V/O: Exposure to manganese is managed as a material risk within our business and we take proactive steps to reduce the risk by applying controls in line with international best practice.

If our workers display any symptoms of occupational illness, we take this very seriously. Appropriate care and support would be provided based on the individual circumstances.

V/O: But the risk of manganese dust exposure isn’t limited to the mines. Coming up in Part 2 - our journey takes us south to Gqeberha - and what we found ......will disturb you.







MANGANESE ROAD

PART 2

V/O: It’s a thousand kilometres from the manganese mines of Hotazel to Gqeberha. Every day, hundreds of trucks criss-cross the route, leaving dust and potholes in their wake. Small towns like Cradock and Middelburg aren’t coping. Noncedo Zonke is the Mayor.

Zonke: They are damaging almost everything: our electric poles, the stop signs. The last straw now is that they is now getting to houses of people whilst people are asleep.

Derek: Mayor, how much has the damage cost the Municipality?

Zonke: Currently we need more than ten million.

V/O: The trucks forge ahead, charging about R33000 per round trip.
Some head straight to the port, but many off-load in a suburb called Markman 20km away, where the manganese is bulk stored. Compared to a few years ago, the area has gone rapidly downhill.

Link: Markman was a typical light industrial area before lockdown. Some companies moved out and the manganese handlers swooped in. This place is really a mess, and it’s hard to think that it can ever recover.

V/O: Only one operator has a licence to bulk store manganese in Markman. The others are operating on land not zoned for noxious use, and the municipality is taking legal action.

Nkosi: There is even an operator directly opposite a food processing facility.

V/O: MT Nkosi is a public health consultant, focusing on food safety and hygiene. His clients in Markman have been hard-hit.

00:08:33 You know, with manganese you are supposed to have dust suppression measures. It’s supposed to be indoors, even the loading of it. So what you would find is they’ve got this mountain of manganese outside. They are loading and there is dust that is just uncontrolled.

V/O: These photos were taken inside the food processing plant. To maintain food safety standards everything requires constant cleaning.

Sfx: Banging filter

The damage to roads is obvious, but Manganese operators say they’re not entirely to blame.

V/O: Chris Collett has a precast concrete products factory in a cul-de sac. Since the manganese operators moved in, over a thousand trucks pass by every day.

Chris: It's really forcing us to think about moving if the situation doesn't change. We also have to nowadays cover most of our products with plastic bags. Where the stuff hasn't been covered, we've then got to wash and double handle product. so it's added cost to our production.

Derek: Just explain how it affects your staff?

Chris: We’re very concerned about the health and welfare of our staff. You know they complain. We don’t really know what to do at this point.

V/O: Environmental scientist Ronelle Friend, conducted small particle dust fallout tests at their premises.

Ronelle: The magnitude of pollution is huge. The values are five times the allowed national standard. So the national standard is 1200mg/m2/day. And what we found here is it’s more than 6000mg/m2/day so five times the national standard is huge.

Link: This is the neighbour that Chris says has affected his business – Black Magic, owned by the former Mr South Africa, Paul Phume, the beauty king.

V/O: Paul Phume invited us to an interview in Markman, but then cancelled. In a written response Black Magic state:

Recent air pollution tests at Chrysler street record the max concentration of manganese is 1185, which is within acceptable limits.

According to our experts that is not correct. The standard is not specifically for manganese, it’s for total dust fallout. The actual manganese is just a quarter of the ore that it’s extracted from. So the total manganese ore particles in the fallout dust is 4 times higher – way over the national standard.


Pause…..
Chris: On the 2nd of August they were still loading their trucks outside? And the dust just goes everywhere.

V/O: But what does this mean for people in the surrounding area?

Sfx: Accordion player

V/O: Up in Gauteng we made a trip to Meyerton where research shows that even low levels of manganese in the air can be dangerous to your health.
This township lies next to South 32’s ferromanganese smelter. Scientists measured manganese levels over a period of 5 years and compared them to a control site with no industrial activity.
00:25:41
Gill: The levels in Meyerton were about 20 times higher than they were in the control site.

V/O: Which may sound bad, but the manganese levels were actually very low. Professor Gill Nelson is from the Wits School of Public Health.

Prof: If you compare them to the occupational exposure level which is 5mg/m3, we’re looking at 203ng/m3. It’s much, much smaller. But one of the conclusions of our research is that even at those low levels there may be some risk of developing parkinsonian signs.

V/O: They tested over 700 people, living within a 5km radius of the smelter, for parkinsonian signs.

Prof: Residents living near the smelter were much slower. So their motor function was affected – much slower than the control population – and their cognitive function was also compromised.

V/O: South32 says:
Community manganese dust levels are monitored and compared against an internationally accepted guidance value. Any exceedances are investigated and action response plans are developed and implemented.

V/O: Meanwhile back in Gqeberha, trucks from Markman carry manganese in open skips to and from the port, 24 hours a day, leaving a trail of pollution.

Derek: How far are you from the port?

Aubrey: As the crow flies probably one kilometre.

V/O: Aubrey du Plessis lives in a suburb called Southend. Like many residents he installed a water tank.

Aubrey: This is unfit for human consumption.

V/O: Rob Francis runs charter tours around Algoa Bay on his catamaran. The yacht club is only a few hundred meters from the manganese ships and manganese dust blankets the boats.

Rob: In the evening the boats get a little bit of dew and then it migrates down to all the horizontal spots and it corrodes – everything that it comes into contact with.

V/O: Ironically, the MMC for Economic Development, Tourism and Agriculture Khusta Jack also has manganese trucks.

Jack: The problem is there’s a demand for manganese. The trains cannot move them. And that’s why you’ve got more than maybe half a million trucks on the road at the moment? That’s not my making Derek.

Derek: That’s not your making. But I think you must admit Khusta, that it’s ethically wrong. Even if it is two or three trucks?

Jack: It could be ethically wrong, but not from where I move from. It’s a market, it’s a business that is there. I got into it. That’s what I did.

V/O: But he’s not the only politician to have jumped on the manganese bandwagon. We had a look at the national picture.

Link: United Manganese of Kalahari is one of the most profitable mines in Hotazel. Financial records show that in 2020 it paid out a staggering R2.4 billion in dividends. Little wonder then that they could afford a small donation of R15 million to the ANC last year.

V/O: The party also received R15 million from Chancellor House, the ANC’s investment vehicle. Chancellor House owns 22% of UMK mine.

Garland: Today, at the request of the United States Department of Justice, Spanish authorities seized a super yacht belonging to a sanctioned Russian oligarch.

V/O: That yacht belonged to Viktor Vekselberg, their joint venture partner. It’s well documented that he owned 49% of UMK until US sanctions forced him to restructure his shareholding.

V/O: UMK says “Vekselberg does not own any direct interest in UMK and is an economic beneficiary of a trust that owns less than 25% of UMK.”

V/O: Chancellor House and the ANC did not respond.

V/O: A new 17million tonne manganese terminal is planned for Nqura, but the Contractor will only be appointed next year. After that, Transnet says: The design and construction will take place for almost four to five years.

V/O: But from what we saw, there won’t be much left of Markman by then.

Prof: Manganese exposure is associated with parkinsonism. Tidu: You could have two persons with the exact same exposure. Nothing will happen to the one and the other one will die. V/O: We saw the queue of trucks waiting to offload at Port Elizabeth harbour. But nothing could prepare us for the hellhole that is Markman, the industrial area where manganese is bulk stored. Chris: What am I going to do? We pay our rates. The roads weren’t like this when we got here. V/O: And we delved into the ownership of the lucrative mines - and discovered a network of Chinese, Australian, and Russian companies with politically influential local partners. V/O: This is the Kalahari Basin – home to 80% of the world’s manganese – a key component of steel and lithium batteries. Mines dotted around Hotazel export millions of tonnes to China every year, earning billions of dollars in export revenue. Link: This is Hotazel, not quite living up to its reputation today, but it is the tail-end of winter. Now, forget the posh office blocks in Sandton, it’s in this far-flung corner of the Kalahari that manganese is creating jobs for thousands and making the mining companies fabulously wealthy. But at what cost? V/O: Manganese is a neurotoxin and excessive exposure to manganese dust or fumes can cause permanent brain damage. Extreme manganese toxicity results in a condition called manganism. Dirk: The tremor started first, but slightly. Like for instance I tried to test on a fuse box, I couldn’t do it anymore because I couldn’t pinpoint on the fuse with the tester. V/O: Dirk Jooste was an auto-electrician, working for a sub-contractor on a mine called Mamatwan. His job was repairing air-conditioners on the big, yellow dump trucks. Dirk: It’s the old triple 7D CAT machines and it’s a very confined space. So I had to clean out those evaporators inside, and the only way to do it was by pressurised air. Because it wasn’t a dust as such, it’s like a powder, and the whole cab was full of that dust so, when I was finished at night my teeth, my tongue, everything was pitch, pitch black inside. Derek: How old were you when the symptoms first started? Dirk: Derek you must excuse me but my memory is a bit…I can remember my childhood and everything, but my short-term memory about everything is not that good. V/O: Extreme manganese toxicity results in a condition called manganism. Dirk: I get angry very quickly, and I wasn’t like that before, never before. V/O: In 2011, at the age of 54, Dirk was diagnosed with Parkinson’s Disease, but the prescribed medication had no effect at all. He also developed blisters on his hands when in contact with manganese. A dermatologist diagnosed severe allergic dermatitis. Dirk: His recommendation was to take me off the mine completely, and also out of our office area, because it also happens there, because there’s also a lot of manganese dust. Derek: How did you feel about leaving the mine area? Dirk: That was my life. My work was my life. It’s taken away. It’s just taken away. V/O: In 2013 he consulted Occupational Practitioner Dr Tidu van der Merwe in Kathu. Tidu: I realised that since he was working in a mining environment that this might not be Parkinson’s but manganism. Manganism, like Parkinson’s, will affect your fine motor skills. So that goes through to balance and activities of everyday life. But getting to the final and conclusive diagnosis that rests with the neurologists. V/O: So, Dr van der Merwe sent Dirk to a neurologist but his findings were inconclusive. Tidu: I’m unsure of the final diagnosis – I’m translating here –it is not suggestive of Parkinson’s Disease. Derek: In 2013 you were convinced Dirk was suffering from severe manganism. Do you stand by that? Tidu: I still stand by that. V/O: But what about the other mineworkers? In 2020 the American Journal of Industrial Medicine published an article on manganese exposure and parkinsonian signs in South African mine workers. The study was a collaboration between Washington University and Wits University. Prof: We went to Hotazel, to the mines. The Union certainly helped us by putting the word out there that we were doing the research. V/O: Associate Professor Gill Nelson is an epidemiologist at the Wits School of Public Health. Prof: We ended up with 187 people eventually, 187 mine workers. So we had people who worked there for a year and then we also had people who’d worked there for, say some close to 40 years. Derek: So what signs did you look for? Gill: So we look for Parkinsonian signs which is tremor at rest, balance and stiffness in joints – the conventional Parkinsonian signs. Derek: What were your findings? Gill: So about 26% of the participants had Parkinsonian signs which is… Derek: It’s high? Gill: It’s very high, we wouldn’t expect that. V/O: The average age of the miners was 42. Derek: How concerning are these results in reality? Prof: So they definitely are concerning, because you shouldn’t have such a high prevalence of parkinsonism in a normal population, so there’s something going on. Link: South32 is an Australian company with a head Office in Sandton. We wanted to talk to them about the health risks of manganese dust exposure, but they said there was nobody in South Africa to interview. So we offered them a Zoom interview from Australia, but all they did was reply in writing. V/O: Exposure to manganese is managed as a material risk within our business and we take proactive steps to reduce the risk by applying controls in line with international best practice. If our workers display any symptoms of occupational illness, we take this very seriously. Appropriate care and support would be provided based on the individual circumstances. V/O: But the risk of manganese dust exposure isn’t limited to the mines. Coming up in Part 2 - our journey takes us south to Gqeberha - and what we found ......will disturb you. MANGANESE ROAD PART 2 V/O: It’s a thousand kilometres from the manganese mines of Hotazel to Gqeberha. Every day, hundreds of trucks criss-cross the route, leaving dust and potholes in their wake. Small towns like Cradock and Middelburg aren’t coping. Noncedo Zonke is the Mayor. Zonke: They are damaging almost everything: our electric poles, the stop signs. The last straw now is that they is now getting to houses of people whilst people are asleep. Derek: Mayor, how much has the damage cost the Municipality? Zonke: Currently we need more than ten million. V/O: The trucks forge ahead, charging about R33000 per round trip. Some head straight to the port, but many off-load in a suburb called Markman 20km away, where the manganese is bulk stored. Compared to a few years ago, the area has gone rapidly downhill. Link: Markman was a typical light industrial area before lockdown. Some companies moved out and the manganese handlers swooped in. This place is really a mess, and it’s hard to think that it can ever recover. V/O: Only one operator has a licence to bulk store manganese in Markman. The others are operating on land not zoned for noxious use, and the municipality is taking legal action. Nkosi: There is even an operator directly opposite a food processing facility. V/O: MT Nkosi is a public health consultant, focusing on food safety and hygiene. His clients in Markman have been hard-hit. 00:08:33 You know, with manganese you are supposed to have dust suppression measures. It’s supposed to be indoors, even the loading of it. So what you would find is they’ve got this mountain of manganese outside. They are loading and there is dust that is just uncontrolled. V/O: These photos were taken inside the food processing plant. To maintain food safety standards everything requires constant cleaning. Sfx: Banging filter The damage to roads is obvious, but Manganese operators say they’re not entirely to blame. V/O: Chris Collett has a precast concrete products factory in a cul-de sac. Since the manganese operators moved in, over a thousand trucks pass by every day. Chris: It's really forcing us to think about moving if the situation doesn't change. We also have to nowadays cover most of our products with plastic bags. Where the stuff hasn't been covered, we've then got to wash and double handle product. so it's added cost to our production. Derek: Just explain how it affects your staff? Chris: We’re very concerned about the health and welfare of our staff. You know they complain. We don’t really know what to do at this point. V/O: Environmental scientist Ronelle Friend, conducted small particle dust fallout tests at their premises. Ronelle: The magnitude of pollution is huge. The values are five times the allowed national standard. So the national standard is 1200mg/m2/day. And what we found here is it’s more than 6000mg/m2/day so five times the national standard is huge. Link: This is the neighbour that Chris says has affected his business – Black Magic, owned by the former Mr South Africa, Paul Phume, the beauty king. V/O: Paul Phume invited us to an interview in Markman, but then cancelled. In a written response Black Magic state: Recent air pollution tests at Chrysler street record the max concentration of manganese is 1185, which is within acceptable limits. According to our experts that is not correct. The standard is not specifically for manganese, it’s for total dust fallout. The actual manganese is just a quarter of the ore that it’s extracted from. So the total manganese ore particles in the fallout dust is 4 times higher – way over the national standard. Pause….. Chris: On the 2nd of August they were still loading their trucks outside? And the dust just goes everywhere. V/O: But what does this mean for people in the surrounding area? Sfx: Accordion player V/O: Up in Gauteng we made a trip to Meyerton where research shows that even low levels of manganese in the air can be dangerous to your health. This township lies next to South 32’s ferromanganese smelter. Scientists measured manganese levels over a period of 5 years and compared them to a control site with no industrial activity. 00:25:41 Gill: The levels in Meyerton were about 20 times higher than they were in the control site. V/O: Which may sound bad, but the manganese levels were actually very low. Professor Gill Nelson is from the Wits School of Public Health. Prof: If you compare them to the occupational exposure level which is 5mg/m3, we’re looking at 203ng/m3. It’s much, much smaller. But one of the conclusions of our research is that even at those low levels there may be some risk of developing parkinsonian signs. V/O: They tested over 700 people, living within a 5km radius of the smelter, for parkinsonian signs. Prof: Residents living near the smelter were much slower. So their motor function was affected – much slower than the control population – and their cognitive function was also compromised. V/O: South32 says: Community manganese dust levels are monitored and compared against an internationally accepted guidance value. Any exceedances are investigated and action response plans are developed and implemented. V/O: Meanwhile back in Gqeberha, trucks from Markman carry manganese in open skips to and from the port, 24 hours a day, leaving a trail of pollution. Derek: How far are you from the port? Aubrey: As the crow flies probably one kilometre. V/O: Aubrey du Plessis lives in a suburb called Southend. Like many residents he installed a water tank. Aubrey: This is unfit for human consumption. V/O: Rob Francis runs charter tours around Algoa Bay on his catamaran. The yacht club is only a few hundred meters from the manganese ships and manganese dust blankets the boats. Rob: In the evening the boats get a little bit of dew and then it migrates down to all the horizontal spots and it corrodes – everything that it comes into contact with. V/O: Ironically, the MMC for Economic Development, Tourism and Agriculture Khusta Jack also has manganese trucks. Jack: The problem is there’s a demand for manganese. The trains cannot move them. And that’s why you’ve got more than maybe half a million trucks on the road at the moment? That’s not my making Derek. Derek: That’s not your making. But I think you must admit Khusta, that it’s ethically wrong. Even if it is two or three trucks? Jack: It could be ethically wrong, but not from where I move from. It’s a market, it’s a business that is there. I got into it. That’s what I did. V/O: But he’s not the only politician to have jumped on the manganese bandwagon. We had a look at the national picture. Link: United Manganese of Kalahari is one of the most profitable mines in Hotazel. Financial records show that in 2020 it paid out a staggering R2.4 billion in dividends. Little wonder then that they could afford a small donation of R15 million to the ANC last year. V/O: The party also received R15 million from Chancellor House, the ANC’s investment vehicle. Chancellor House owns 22% of UMK mine. Garland: Today, at the request of the United States Department of Justice, Spanish authorities seized a super yacht belonging to a sanctioned Russian oligarch. V/O: That yacht belonged to Viktor Vekselberg, their joint venture partner. It’s well documented that he owned 49% of UMK until US sanctions forced him to restructure his shareholding. V/O: UMK says “Vekselberg does not own any direct interest in UMK and is an economic beneficiary of a trust that owns less than 25% of UMK.” V/O: Chancellor House and the ANC did not respond. V/O: A new 17million tonne manganese terminal is planned for Nqura, but the Contractor will only be appointed next year. After that, Transnet says: The design and construction will take place for almost four to five years. V/O: But from what we saw, there won’t be much left of Markman by then. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Manganese mining - huge profits, but at what cost to our health, environment and infrastructure
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Dirk Jooste is an auto-electrician who was medically boarded at the age of 52. He developed Parkinsonian symptoms or manganism after spending 2 years cleaning air conditioner filters on trucks on Mamatwan mine in Hotazel. Both he and his Occupational Practitioner, Dr Tidu van der Merwe will be interviewed. Manganese is a neurotoxin which is known to cause Parkinsonian symptoms in mine workers with prolonged exposure. Washington University and Wits School pf Public Health published a recent study which found that these symptoms were common in the cohort of 178 miners in Hotazel. Professor Gill Nelson of Wits School of Public Health will discus the study.
metadata.Summary: South Africa produces 80% of the world's manganese, with most of it being exported to China. Millions of tonnes of manganese are transported by road from Hotazel to Nelson Mandela Bay where they are stored in the light industrial area of Markman, before being transferred to Port Elizabeth Harbour by truck in open skips. The dust levels in Markman are already 5 times over the "Take drastic action now" levels. Tests for fugitive dust levels at the entrance to the Port Elizabeth harbour are currently underway. Ronelle Friend from EnviroQuest will discuss the findings. Are locals who live and work in NMB exposed to unacceptable health risks and what are the authorities doing about it? Markman is also home to the Fresh Produce Market as well as the city's abattoir. Other businesses in the area have suffered financial losses because of the dust fallout. Apart from the health risks there are other environmental considerations: the heavy metals found flowing into the Swartkops Estuary is 6000 times higher than the legal limit. Residents complain about manganese dust in their Jojo tanks which has washed off their roofs and gutters. The find, powder-like dust clogs their swimming pool filters and air conditioners. Tourism is also affected. The Port Elizabeth small boat harbour berths several fishing boats which moor under a cloud of manganese dust. The tourist boats as well as every other sailing yacht in the harbour are discoloured by the black dust. The MSC cruise ships also dock in the harbour and passengers are forced to walk through and breathe in the manganese dust which is all pervasive. Ironically the MMC for Tourism and Economic Development, Khusta Jack, has admitted that he has a trucking company which is also transporting manganese.
metadata.Further information: Enormous political and financial interests are at stake. United Manganese of Kalahari is one of the biggest mines in Hotazel, and is owned by a joint venture which includes Chancellor House - an investment company which funds the ANC - as well as sanctioned Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg, through his company Renova. One of the richest men in the world, Vekselberg's plane and super yacht were recently seized by European authorities. In 2020 Chancellor House's 22% dividend would have paid out R528 million. This could explain why there is political influence brought to bear on the traffic and law enforcement authorities to give the manganese transporters and manganese handlers a free pass. Hundreds of trucks travel to PE harbour and back every day, 24 hours a day to satisfy the demand for manganese. The national, regional and urban road network is being destroyed by these heavy loads which average over 50 tonnes per truck. Truck drivers are paid per load and are therefore compelled to work long hours with very little sleep. They live in their trucks, only going home every 3 weeks. They are tired, stressed and in many cases suffering from occupational diseases like high blood pressure and diabetes.
